It is called a **threnody**, though that is only a human convenience. On its world it has no name, because nothing there speaks.

The planet is a cold, iron-heavy world with no true surface weather. Under a sky of frozen ammonia haze, the “sea” is a slow ocean of supercritical fluid—part liquid metal, part dense gas—pressing through fractured crust at depths where rock behaves like warm wax. Light barely matters. Heat leaks up from radioactive decay and from the slow flexing of the planet’s magnetic field. That is what the threnody eats.

It is not an animal in any Earth sense. It has no cells, no skin, no organs, no inside distinct from outside. What you would call its body is a temporary coherence: long, knotted chains of metal-organic molecules drifting in the fluid, held in pattern by standing electromagnetic waves rather than by membranes or skeletons. When the field is strong, the threnody is a thin, kilometers-wide sheet, almost transparent, rippling through the crustal channels like a thought moving through stone. When the field weakens, it collapses into a dense knot no larger than a boulder, and can remain that way for centuries without being dead. Death, for it, is loss of phase—when the waves fall out of step and the knots unwind into ordinary chemistry.

Its “genes” are not a code written in a molecule. Information lives in two places at once: the topology of those molecular knots, and the timing relationships among the magnetic domains that stabilize them. A threnody does not copy itself. It *tunes*. When two coherences drift through the same fracture and their oscillations become commensurate—locked, for a while, into a shared rhythm—they shed a third pattern, a daughter coherence that peels away along a pressure gradient. There are no sexes, no parents in any lasting sense. Lineage is a history of resonances.

It does not see. It registers shear in the fluid, tiny changes in isotope ratios, and the curl of magnetic field lines the way a terrestrial animal registers light and scent. A migrating ore body is, to it, a bright moving shape. A quake is a shout. Other threnodies appear as chords: compatible, dissonant, or dangerous. What we would call thought is a rearrangement of those chords, slow enough that a single decision may outlast a human civilization. It does not experience urgency. It experiences weather.

It has no mouth. Nutrition is catalytic. As the planet’s field breathes, metal complexes in the fluid are nudged through energy states; the threnody’s lattice steers those reactions so that disorder increases outside the pattern and order is preserved inside it. Waste is not excreted. It is a change in the local isotope balance, a faint metallic aftertaste in the rock that can linger for millennia. Geologists from another world, if any ever came, might map ancient threnody paths as inexplicable veins.

Sometimes a threnody sleeps in stone. It settles into a fracture, lets its field slacken, and leaves only a lattice of inclusions—crystals whose defects encode the knot-pattern. In that state it is indistinguishable from unusual mineralogy. A later pulse of magnetism, or the slow arrival of another coherence, can wake it. Individuals in this sense are optional. A threnody can split into many weakly coupled sheets that still count, to themselves, as one, or many knots can phase-lock into a single vast chord that has never existed before. The boundary of a self is a matter of bandwidth.

Nothing about it is bilateral, radial, or even stably shaped. It does not locomote with limbs. It biases the flow around it, riding pressure and field gradients the way a ripple rides a drumhead. It does not fear predators in the animal way; incompatible coherences can detune it, unmaking the pattern without violence. Its closest analog to pain is dissonance. Its closest analog to beauty is a lock that holds.

If you stood in that crushing fluid—which you could not—you would not see a creature. You might, with the right instruments, notice a region where the magnetic hiss of the planet had become briefly musical, and where the chemistry of the rock had been edited with impossible patience. That music, and that editing, would be the animal.
